name: Gyobutsuji Zen Monastery
technique: Shikantaza (just sitting) zazen; monthly five-day liturgy-free sesshin; daily work practice (samu) and study of Dogen Zenji's writings.
teacherAccess: Resident teacher Shoryu Bradley gives a Dharma talk each Saturday and is available to resident practitioners through daily monastic life; sesshins follow the liturgy-free Uchiyama style without formal dokusan interviews.
retreatOptions: Open-ended residential stays for visiting practitioners joining the daily monastic schedule, plus a five-day sesshin held monthly except February and August.
about: Gyobutsuji (Practice Buddha Temple) is a small, off-grid Soto Zen monastery in the Boston Mountains of the Ozarks near Kingston, Arkansas, founded by Shoryu Bradley, a Dharma heir of Shohaku Okumura Roshi. Practice centers on shikantaza (just sitting) zazen in the liturgy-free style of Kosho Uchiyama Roshi, alongside study of Dogen Zenji's writings and daily work practice (samu). Visiting practitioners are welcome to join the full monastic schedule for extended residential stays, sharing zazen, meals, and work with the resident community. Gyobutsuji also holds a five-day sesshin every month except February and August, consisting of fourteen 50-minute periods of zazen daily without dokusan or formal liturgy. The temple, reached only by unpaved mountain roads, is supported entirely by donations, with no charge for lodging, meals, or sesshin attendance.
schedule: Weekday schedule of zazen from 4:40am wake-up through 8:30pm with work periods, study, and meals; five-day sesshin held monthly (except February and August) consisting of fourteen 50-minute zazen periods daily without liturgy or dokusan.
cost: No charge for lodging, meals, or sesshin attendance; the monastery is supported entirely by donations (dana).

pricePerDay.notes: No suggested amount; some supporters make a recurring monthly offering to help the temple budget for meals and upkeep.

foodNotes: Communal breakfast, lunch, and supper are part of the daily monastic schedule; the specific dietary style is not published on the site.
workNotes: Visiting residents join the full monastic schedule, including daily work periods (soji) such as cooking, cleaning, and land upkeep, alongside zazen.
